title: Cooking at the eclipse
hookLine: at Kurukshetra Nanak cooked food on an eclipse day, and tradition says he answered the objections with a hymn

cards: A huge crowd at a holy place. Pilgrims have come from far and wide to bathe and pray, on a day when the sun is about to go dark. Everyone is waiting, watching the sky.
And in the middle of it all, a traveler lights a cooking fire. Today: Kurukshetra.

teach.b: The place was Kurukshetra, a holy site where pilgrims gathered on the day of a solar eclipse to bathe and pray. The custom there held that no food should be cooked while the eclipse lasted.

teach.h: A COOKING FIRE IN THE CROWD.
teach.b: In the tellings, Guru Nanak and Mardana arrive, set up camp near the crowd, and Nanak starts a fire and begins to cook. Some tellings say the food was meat, given to him by a visitor. Smoke rises.
People notice. Priests and pilgrims gather, upset, and the argument begins: why would anyone cook on this of all days?
Tradition says the Guru answered not with a lecture but with a hymn. The Guru Granth Sahib holds a hymn that tradition links to this moment.

In paraphrase, it says that fools quarrel over flesh, but understand nothing of wisdom or meditation. Some readers hear it turning the question away from what's on the fire and toward what's in the heart.
Now notice how Nanak questions the custom. He doesn't shout from a distance or mock people at prayer. He does one small, visible thing, lets it raise the question, and then sings.
The crowd comes to him, curious and angry, and leaves with something to think about. We've seen this before on his road.

teach.h: ASK WHAT A PRACTICE IS FOR.
teach.b: He questioned rituals he thought had lost their meaning, in more than one tradition, and he did it by asking what a practice is for. Sikh teaching carries that on: what matters is the inner truth a custom points to.
Today's story isn't a verdict on the pilgrims.
It's a picture of how to question kindly, in the middle of a crowd.

how: Sikhs tell the Kurukshetra sakhi as an example of Guru Nanak questioning rituals by asking what they are for, and Sikh teaching places inner truth above outward observance.

games.q: you're at Kurukshetra on an eclipse day. the custom says no cooking. you think the custom has lost its meaning. what do you do?
o: stay quiet and keep the custom.
stand up and denounce the crowd.
light a fire, let people come, and answer with a hymn.
games.why: in the tellings, Nanak cooked, the crowd gathered, and tradition says he answered with a hymn about fools who quarrel over flesh but know nothing of wisdom or meditation.

practice: Find one small habit of your own that you keep without knowing why, a lucky shirt, knocking on wood, not saying a hope out loud in case it breaks, and don't sneer at it.
Ask it gently what it's for, what it's trying to protect, and whether there's a truer way to protect that. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you ask.

carryVoice: Your line: kindly, question it. With curiosity, never with scorn. A week on the road, done.
